cases.title: Brunete drew Spanish, Italian and German fighters into the battle
cases.mission: Four Republican I-16 and two I-15 squadrons faced three Nationalist-side Fiat squadrons at the opening. The later arrival of Grupo Morato and German 2./J 88 belongs to a separate stage.
cases.effect: Italian correspondence records Kindelán’s commendation of Italian fighters in the opening days and further requests for air support. This establishes that ground and air commands valued their intervention during the battle.
cases.limit: Salas gives three opposing Fiat squadrons at the opening. The Italian unit chronology puts Nos. 19 and 20 at Torrijos-Barcience and treats No. 18 as a later arrival. A time-stamped field return is needed to place the third squadron on the first night and to identify all six Republican units.

cases.title: Soviet pilots in Republican service met night bombers at Brunete
cases.mission: At the close of the battle, Yakushin and Serov flew night interceptions with Eriomenko’s I-15 squadron. Salas separates their squadron from the Republican I-16 unit then at Santander.
cases.effect: Salas records a German Ju 52 lost on the night of 25/26 July and a Spanish Ju 52 on 26 July. Serov subsequently took command of a night-fighter squadron.
cases.limit: Each pilot claimed one victory. The historian’s chronology does not establish which pilot destroyed which aircraft or whether both losses had the same cause.

cases.title: Tremp escort and the loss of the Natachas
cases.mission: Grupo 21’s 6ª and 7ª Escuadrillas took off at 14:45 with ten and nine fighters respectively to cover nine Natachas of Grupo 30’s 2ª Escuadrilla on the Llimiana mission.
cases.effect: The Republican fighter diary records the escort. Survivor evidence places only three bombers back on friendly fields. Nationalist 2G3’s record independently places two attached pilots in combat. Republican command subsequently relieved the 7ª commander over the separation.
cases.limit: The Nationalist account records attacks, including one broken off without a visible result. Neither side supplies a reliable individual attacker for every missing bomber.

Republican.effort: Six opening fighter squadrons by type, a named I-15 squadron with Soviet pilots later at Brunete, and two December escort squadrons at Tremp.
Republican.losses: The nine-aircraft bomber sortie has three documented returns to friendly fields. Fighter losses for the campaign remain open.
Republican.effect: Survivor accounts and command action document the consequences of the break in escort.

Nationalist.effort: The Italian chronology names two initial and four arriving squadrons. Spanish and German accounts identify other reinforcements, with the opening third Fiat squadron unresolved.
Nationalist.losses: The 2G3 combat account describes attacks, including one without an observed outcome. A complete reciprocal loss ledger is missing.
Nationalist.effect: Italian and Spanish command correspondence documents demand for air support. The Tremp accounts establish contact without allocating every bomber loss.

cases.title: Warsaw’s defenders dispersed one formation while bombs reached Jabłonna
cases.mission: The Pursuit Brigade scrambled III/1 and IV/1 Dywizjony. Its four organic escadrilles and attached 123rd are distinct from the 152nd, which assisted later. German 5. and 6.(K)/LG 1 met fighters while 4.(K)/LG 1 bombed Ciechanów.
cases.effect: By 16:00 Pawlikowski reported that one formation scattered on seeing III/1 while IV/1 saw three aircraft drop bombs on Jabłonna. The different observations explain why the same day contains both a local disruption and a completed bombing.
cases.limit: The 16:00 Polish return lists one missing, one heavily damaged, one moderately damaged and eleven lightly damaged aircraft. A full-day loss return is still needed. Visual sightings do not identify the fate of each German bomber.

cases.title: Interception over Warsaw and damage at Okęcie
cases.mission: Pilots of 111 and 112 Eskadry from Zielonka encountered the Bf 110s of I.(Z)/LG 1 covering III.(K)/LG 1. A separate air-warning message recorded damage at Okęcie.
cases.effect: The contemporary message distinguished the airframe works, which stopped operating, from the engine factory, which could continue. Contact by the Polish fighters and loss of production can both be traced on the day.
cases.limit: The reporting chains locate the engagement and the damage in the same operational area. They do not identify which crew dropped the bomb that stopped the works.

cases.title: Slovak fighters supported the southern front
cases.mission: Two Slovak fighter detachments provided cover for German dive bombers from Kamenica nad Cirochou. Elements of 37. letka arrived on 9 September. Accounts disagree about which other unit arrived on 7 September.
cases.effect: The two units flew eight escort missions in the account Baka compares. On 9 September antiaircraft fire forced a 37. letka aircraft down. Grúň returned to Slovak lines on 12 September after his capture and escape.
cases.limit: Raininec gives the earlier unit as 39/12. Emmerling, using Freiburg records, gives 49/13. The disagreement leaves one of the two identities open. No ground recipient records the effect of those eight escorts here.

cases.title: Warsaw’s Pursuit Brigade withdrew to the Lublin area
cases.mission: IPN follows the brigade through Zaborów and Radzików on 4–6 September, then to the Lublin area from 7 September. Its sorties could no longer be counted as fighters operating from the capital’s opening fields.
cases.effect: IPN’s table distinguishes own aircraft destroyed and damaged in the Lublin phase. Its separate victory column records claims. This places losses and continued fighting after the withdrawal.
cases.limit: The table covers eleven days near Lublin. It does not identify a sortie date for each loss or give the serviceability of every aircraft moved.

Allied.effort: The Pursuit Brigade report and Army Modlin account document distinct morning and afternoon participation.
Allied.losses: The commander’s 16:00 report tracks the first day. IPN later distinguishes destroyed and damaged aircraft by airfield and period, including the move to Lublin.
Allied.effect: A formation dispersed in front of III/1. Jabłonna was bombed, and a separate 3 September report documents a shutdown at the Okęcie airframe works.

Axis.effort: Three German bomber Staffeln and a separate fighter sweep are identifiable on 1 September. Of two later Slovak fighter detachments at Kamenica, one has competing identifications.
Axis.losses: A Slovak fighter force-landed on 9 September and its pilot later escaped. German losses claimed by the Pursuit Brigade remain incompletely matched.
Axis.effect: One Staffel bombed Ciechanów while the others met Polish fighters. Slovak fighter escort is documented without a measured ground result.

cases.title: The Norwegian Army’s fighters met the invasion over Oslo
cases.mission: Seven Gladiators of Jagervingen scrambled from Fornebu against incoming German aircraft. The Norwegian airframe history follows Gladiator 427 into combat with a Dornier Do 17.
cases.effect: Both machines force-landed, 427 near Kolsås and the Dornier near Bryn church. Its crew burned the German aircraft. Other Norwegian fighters landed at different locations as the defence broke up.
cases.limit: The serial-level history establishes this pair of dispositions. The formation’s wider reported victories still require matching German loss returns.

cases.title: Shore-based naval aircraft sank Königsberg in Bergen
cases.mission: Skua dive bombers of 800 and 803 Naval Air Squadrons flew from Hatston against the German cruiser, which had remained in Bergen after gunfire damage the previous day.
cases.effect: The British naval diary recorded the attack. The independently written German Naval Staff diary placed the dive bombing at 08:00, described two bomb hits and fire, and recorded that the abandoned cruiser capsized at 11:00. The surviving crew joined the coastal defences.
cases.limit: The German diary’s two reported hits belong to its own account. The ship’s later fate is firmer than any assignment of a specific hit to one British crew.

cases.title: Land-based patrols during the recapture of Narvik
cases.mission: RAF Nos. 263 and 46 Squadrons patrolled the battle area from Bardufoss. The Air Historical Branch counted 42 and 53 operational flights respectively and at most three aircraft airborne at once.
cases.effect: French troops entered Narvik and the Poles reached Beisfjord while the patrols continued. The forward base sustained cover during the assault. The campaign narrative then records the start of the already ordered evacuation.
cases.limit: The reconstructed squadron record says Williams broke off short of fuel after observing smoke from a He 111 attacking a cruiser. Milligan’s evening attack had no visible result. Neither entry establishes a German write-off or that the whole assault depended on the patrols.

Allied.effort: Norwegian Army fighters, Norwegian naval aviation, shore- and carrier-launched British naval aircraft and the Bardufoss RAF squadrons can be distinguished.
Allied.losses: Fornebu airframe records follow individual Gladiators. A coalition-wide loss total with common damage criteria remains open.
Allied.effect: The Bergen sinking has a German recipient record. The 28 May patrols coincided with the Allied assault at Narvik.

Axis.effort: Gaul’s schedule identifies two initial fighter groups, an additional group on 15 April, and eleven initial level- or dive-bomber groups.
Axis.losses: The German naval diary establishes the loss of Königsberg. The Grotli account identifies a specific He 111. Neither gives theatre-wide aircraft losses.
Axis.effect: The cruiser’s surviving crew transferred to coastal defence. The sortie from Ark Royal can be tied to the interruption of one German bombing attack.

cases.title: Three Belgian escorts met German fighters over Vroenhoven
cases.mission: Three Gladiators from the first platoon of Belgian 1/I/2 flew cover for Fairey Battles assigned to the bridges. Fighters of I./JG 1 intercepted them.
cases.effect: Rolin escaped by parachute, Pirlot died, and Vandenbroek returned to Beauvechain with his Gladiator damaged. The German formation had removed two of the three escorts. A third had actually returned.
cases.limit: Decobeck reconstructed the encounter decades later using the participants’ accounts. Their shared chronology does not establish that the loss of escort caused any particular Battle bomber loss.

cases.title: The RAF’s six Hurricane squadrons changed meaning in one day
cases.mission: On 9 May the Air Component had four Hurricane squadrons. The AASF’s Nos. 1 and 73 bring the British total in France to six. Nos. 3 and 79 joined the Air Component on 10 May and No. 504 on 11 May.
cases.effect: The evening of 10 May therefore yields six in the Air Component alone. By 16 May Dowding described ten squadron-equivalents dispatched in recent days when arguing about the demands on home defence.
cases.limit: The four squadron-equivalents ordered on 16 May came from eight different squadrons. Six flights crossed that day and two the next. Neither Dowding’s ten nor the order’s four should become a count of complete named units in France.

cases.title: Polish fighters from Dreux challenged an escorted bomber raid
cases.mission: Seventeen pilots of GC I/145 scrambled, according to Pawlak. The unit held part of the Seine defence sector under Groupement 42. Its slow-climbing Caudrons had missed earlier interceptions.
cases.effect: On this occasion the pilots reached the raid and sustained fatalities. The roster identifies Lech Lachowicki-Czechowicz among those killed. The group subsequently moved away from Dreux on 11 June.
cases.limit: The accounts give estimates of the opposing force and Polish victory claims. No matched German loss return establishes how many bombers the attack destroyed or turned back.

Allied.effort: Named French, Dutch, Belgian, Polish and RAF formations have separate command and date boundaries.
Allied.losses: Vroenhoven yields three escort aircraft outcomes. The Polish roster identifies individual fatalities. French, Dutch and British returns still need a common daily basis.
Allied.effect: At Schiphol some fighters refuelled and flew again. Survivors regrouped at Buiksloot. Belgian escort losses can be traced through the aircraft that actually returned.

Axis.effort: The Luftflotte 2 table identifies seven Bf 109 and four Bf 110 Gruppen in one fighter-command section. Other corps and Luftflotte 3 enlarge the theatre total.
Axis.losses: German assignments and combined headquarters strength do not identify losses. The June Polish claims lack reciprocal German loss returns.
Axis.effect: I./JG 1 removed two of three Belgian escorts over Vroenhoven. Evidence for the bridge strike itself belongs to the bomber and recipient records.

cases.title: Fighter escorts reached London while RAF units fought and guarded their bases
cases.mission: I. Fliegerkorps tasked JG 26, JG 54 and JG 27 with bomber escort, and ZG 76 with clearing the target area. No. 249 Squadron attacked the raid. Canadian No. 1 was kept on station defence apart from McNab’s individual interception.
cases.effect: The Admiralty independently recorded serious fires in the East India, West India, Surrey Commercial and Millwall docks. No. 249’s formation could not see what damage its attack caused. A separate pilot claimed a Dornier, and Beard bailed out of a Hurricane.
cases.limit: The German order gives intended assignments, the RAF records give observed contact, and the docks report gives the result on the ground. Individual bomb damage cannot be allocated to a particular escorted formation.

cases.title: Actual departures differed from the day’s station list
cases.mission: The war-station table places British No. 1 at Heath Row and No. 79 at Biggin Hill. No. 1’s intelligence report documents eleven taking off from Northolt. No. 79’s diary records departure from Croydon.
cases.effect: The pilots’ reports establish two actual launch fields for the evening. No. 79 engaged over Maidstone–Dartford. In No. 1 the main group missed contact while two separated pilots encountered bombers.
cases.limit: The accounts address different events. The departure evidence does not establish a formal transfer of either whole squadron or the location of every flight throughout the day.

cases.title: Scramble orders, airborne reinforcements and a bomber at Victoria Station
cases.mission: No. 11 Group ordered eleven squadrons up between 11:05 and 11:20. The five No. 12 Group squadrons airborne at 11:25 included Polish No. 302 and Czechoslovak No. 310. The museum also reproduces a combat report from a No. 72 pilot.
cases.effect: A No. 504 Squadron Hurricane flown by Ray Holmes collided with a Dornier which fell at Victoria Station. Some bombers nevertheless dropped their loads in central London. The museum records further fighter attacks during their return.
cases.limit: A dated order does not prove that every unit made contact. The No. 72 pilot saw hits on a fighter but lost sight of it. That report alone cannot establish destruction.

Allied.effort: Six 7 September squadron records distinguish guarding, contact and launch. The 15 September chronology distinguishes scramble orders from airborne status.
Allied.losses: Beard’s damaged Hurricane and bailout are reported by No. 249. No. 72’s later observation of hits gives no verified German loss.
Allied.effect: The Admiralty records fires in four dock systems. The museum ties a single 15 September interception to the Dornier that fell at Victoria Station.

Axis.effort: A contemporary I. Fliegerkorps order specifies three bomber wings, three escort wings and a separate clearance wing. It supplies no actual sortie count.
Axis.losses: The British accounts contain claims and isolated aircraft outcomes. They do not reconstruct each German wing’s losses or repairable damage.
Axis.effect: London docks sustained major fires despite interception. No witness assigns the damage at each dock to one German wing.
